studies.title: house studies
paragraphs: This study brings together a curated selection of residential buildings to explore how architectural composition shapes spatial organization and, ultimately, spatial experience. The houses included in this research come from a wide range of geographical and cultural contexts—spanning Europe, North America, Latin America and India. Despite these differences in climate, culture and time period, the projects share an important common thread: they are influential architectural works in which compositional strategies play a central role in shaping form, space and movement.

The selection of houses was guided primarily by the clarity with which each project reveals its compositional logic. In some cases, the organization of space emerges through geometric order and strong axial systems; in others, it is shaped by relationships with the landscape, spatial sequencing, structural expression, or the atmospheric use of light and colour. Rather than attempting to compile a comprehensive catalogue of houses, the intention was to assemble a focused set of examples where compositional principles are clearly legible and can be meaningfully compared. Projects that lacked sufficient documentation or where the compositional intent remained ambiguous were therefore excluded from the study.

This research approaches the houses through the lens of composition as an architectural language. Instead of analysing them only within stylistic or historical categories, the projects are understood as composed spatial systems—arrangements of volumes, planes, axes and hierarchies that structure spatial experience. Seen in this way, each house demonstrates how architectural composition functions as an ordering framework, guiding movement, shaping relationships between spaces, and influencing how form is perceived. Across different cultural contexts and architectural ideologies, domestic architecture repeatedly turns to a limited set of compositional strategies to organize space.

Methodologically, the study involves a process of reading, decoding and representing architectural compositions. Each house is examined through plans, sections and analytical diagrams in order to identify compositional elements such as axes, grids, hierarchies and spatial sequences. As part of this process, drawings with red and blue overlays are produced to decode compositional relationships. These diagrams make visible structural alignments, spatial hierarchies and circulation patterns, revealing the underlying order that governs each project.

Revisiting composition across such a broad historical range feels particularly relevant today, when architectural discourse often emphasizes technology, performance and digital form-making. By contrast, this study foregrounds the enduring importance of composition as one of architecture's most fundamental tools—through which space, form and experience are structured.

This publication represents the first volume of the research, documenting and analysing twenty houses that demonstrate diverse compositional approaches within domestic architecture. Conceived as an ongoing body of work, future volumes will expand the collection and continue to examine additional houses across different contexts and time periods.

studies.title: margin studies
paragraphs: Margins in architecture refer to the spatial edges or intermediate zones that exist between built form and surrounding context. Rather than acting merely as boundaries, these margins organize transitions between spaces and structure the relationship between interior and exterior environments. Through their placement and composition, margins often dictate physical access, guiding entry, movement and spatial hierarchy. While they vary greatly in form, scale and program, they share a common condition: the margin is not treated as a residual or leftover space but as an active spatial device.

The buildings selected for this study, margins appear in the form of courtyards, arcades, plazas, forecourts or circulation corridors—spaces that mediate between built form and open environment, interior and exterior, or collective and individual realms.

The primary criterion for selecting these works was the clarity with which margins shape the compositional order of space. In several historical religious complexes, the courtyard acts as a spatial margin that organizes the relationship between architecture, congregation and landscape. In modern urban contexts, large public plazas operate as civic margins that structure the interface between built blocks and collective movement. Similarly, courtyard-based domestic typologies demonstrate how margins can structure everyday life, mediating between interior living spaces and the surrounding environment.

Methodologically, the research involves a process of reading and decoding. It then represents the spatial analysis through red blue drawings. Examining to identify relationships between center and edge, therefore interior and exterior. These drawings reveal the intent behind the composition and its effects on the space enclosed.

While margins play a critical role in shaping the politics of access and exclusion within the built environment, this study deliberately sets aside their political implications in order to focus on their compositional and spatial intent. The political dimension of margins is significant enough to be chapterized separately as a series in the study.

Part One of this study focuses on Indo Islamic architecture. Architectural elements such as courtyards, gateways, arcades and forecourts create layered thresholds that mediate between the exterior and interior.

studies.title: kangra studies
paragraphs: Meaning is generally Kangra Studies begins with the Kangra Fort, once impregnable and now in ruin. Drawn at 1:50, each stone is delineated to foreground construction and surface over outline. While the drawings record the fort in its present state, accompanying texts trace its journey as it changed hands and power.

The study attempts to draw a visual atlas of the physical artefacts of varying scales, from the crafted personal to the constructed urban. The idea is to create a repository in the drawing form of all such articles which have informed its character. This way, the reading of a place can be extracted through the visual archive as much as the recorded fact. These drawings can then be used to inform patterns and tendencies for the context.

Kangra Fort, or Nagarkot, the first part of the study, is approached not as a finished building, but as an artefact in flux. It is read through its fragments, surfaces, thresholds, and absences. Each element conveys a sense of time to the contextual study, revealed through construction. The palimpsest that emerges is read as a character of the built artefact, marking an important distinction between craft and construction.

Today, as the question of modern conservation looms, the fort stands for an idea of the architectural project as the act of building; one in which additions appear as dialog in material form. Therefore the attempt is to record the physical presence of the artefact in drawings that reveal these constructional relationships.
